newsitem.title: JAPAN: BOJ catches market off-guard, checks rate rises.
newsitem.headline: BOJ catches market off-guard, checks rate rises.

text.p: In a surprise move, the Bank of Japan (BOJ) sent a clear signal on Friday that it will hold on to its ultra-easy credit stance for a while, even as the market speculated that it may be readying for a mild tightening.
The central bank caught the money market off-guard when it injected 200 billion yen into the market, even though banks only needed 100 billion yen to make up a shortfall.
It was the first time the BOJ had conducted an accommodative money market operation since August 7, 1996.
The benchmark overnight call rate fell to 0.48 percent after the BOJ's action from Thursday's weighted average of 0.53 percent, the highest since April 9, 1996.
"The (central) bank conducted an accommodative money market operation in order to help lower the key overnight call rate," a BOJ official told Reuters.
The official also said the operation was within commitments the bank announced in September 1995.
On September 8, 1995, the BOJ cut the official discount rate (ODR) to a record low 0.5 percent and said the overnight call rate should move slightly below the ODR on average.

In the foreign exchange and money market, some traders had speculated that the BOJ was getting ready for a mild credit tightening in view of the recent recoveries in capital spending and strong export growth.
The key overnight call rate rose as high as to 0.55 percent on Thursday from 0.48 percent earlier this month.
The dollar has been weaker against the yen partly due to active yen purchases by U.S. speculative funds on recent rises in Japan's money rates and strong economic data.
"If it were a neutral operation, the key overnight call rate could have shot up to 0.55 percent," said a senior money dealer at a city bank.
On Thursday, although some operators had expected the BOJ to conduct an accommodative operation like today's, the BOJ injected just enough funds to offset a market shortage.
This triggered a view, albeit briefly, that the BOJ might let the key overnight rate rise before confirming any policy change in an announcement, money traders said.
But Friday's accommodative operation relieved the market as it showed that the BOJ was not yet ready to allow the key overnight rate to rise above 0.50 percent, they said.

"What has been happening in the money market is a fight between the BOJ and major banks which want to take advantage of the BOJ's low interest rate policy and raise funds mainly at the short-end of the market," the senior money dealer said.
Given that the BOJ is keeping its commitments, many banks preferred to raise funds at the short end of the market, although traders said demand was rising ahead of the fiscal year-end.
